title: Americans Want Cars That Work Like Smartphones
paragraphs: We use our smartphones for almost everything these days. They help us find directions, pay for things, listen to music, and keep in touch with friends and family.
So why shouldn't our cars be able to do the same?
According to a new survey, that's exactly what many American drivers are expecting from their next vehicle.
A survey commissioned by technology company Verra Mobility asked 2,000 US drivers in May about something called "connected vehicle technology."
The survey defined this technology as something that allows cars to access digital services through their own built-in communication systems, without needing to connect to a smartphone.

The survey found that 72% of respondents expect their next car to come with this technology, including built-in apps and digital services. And 51% said connected technology could influence which vehicle they choose next.
So what exactly do drivers want their cars to do?

Many said they're interested in technology that makes everyday journeys easier — for example, a car that could suggest nearby parking spaces, gas stations or charging points, or help with toll payments.
About half of participants said they would feel comfortable letting their car automatically pay for parking and road tolls.

Younger drivers are particularly interested in connected vehicle technology. Among drivers ages 18 to 24, 67% already use at least one connected service that was included with their car, compared with 44% of those ages 55 to 64.
However, not everyone is comfortable with how much information these vehicles collect.

Although 66% say they would share driving and location data in exchange for benefits such as insurance discounts or automatic payments, only 14% say they fully understand what information their car collects. And more than half say they are concerned about vehicle data collection practices.
So while many Americans want their cars to become smarter and more convenient, they still have questions about what happens to their personal information once they turn the engine on.
